extracted.intended_audience: metalworkers, refiners, miners, and agricultural practitioners (saffron growers) / 17th-century technical readership
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, procedural instructions and observations for producing and processing metals (iron, tin, lead white, refined gold) and for saffron cultivation/processing, including tooling, furnace/ kiln design, materials, timing, and expected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brush-ore identification and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The best iron-ore (called 'brush-ore') is of a bluish colour, very ponderous and full of little shining specks, like grains of silver; it affords the greatest quantity of iron but, melted alone, produces metal very short and brittle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize ore by colour, weight and shining specks; do not melt brush-ore alone for common use because it produces brittle iron — it must be treated/mixed appropriately (see use of cinder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cinder (refuse ore) to improve iron toughness
rubrics_metrics.description: To remedy the brittleness when brush-ore is melted alone, workmen mix it with 'cinder' (the refuse of ore after metal extraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix cinder with brush-ore in due quantity to produce an 'excellent temper of toughness' for which the Forest of Dean iron is preferred; cinder is plentiful where former works stood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calcining iron ore in kilns prior to smelting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ore is calcined in kilns much after the fashion of ordinary lime-kilns: fill kilns with alternate strata of coal and ore, kindle at the bottom, burn till coal is wasted, renew and repeat. This is done without fusion of the metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to consume drossy parts and make ore friable to facilitate subsequent beating and washing. Kilns are filled and re-fired in cycles rather than melted; follow strata filling and controlled burning to avoid fusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blast-furnace design and operation (dimensions, bellows, casting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Furnaces built of brick or stone ~24 feet square outside and near 30 feet in height; interior not above 8–10 feet at widest (egg-like shape). Two huge pairs of bellows behind furnace operated by a water-wheel via buttons and counterpoise weights; receivers at bottom to collect molten metal; sand bed with furrows for casting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operate bellows alternately so one blasts while the other rises; keep furnaces constantly employed for many months (never let fire slacken). Use receivers to remove scum and dross; pour molten iron into prepared sand furrows while metal remains very fluid and boiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel choice: charcoal remains necessary (sea-coal ineffective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charcoal is used in the furnaces and forges; attempts to introduce sea-coal have proved ineffectual because sea-coal fires, however vehement, will not penetrate the most fixed parts of the ore, leaving much metal unmelted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer charcoal despite cost; be wary of switching to sea-coal as it may reduce yield of melted metal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finery and chafery forge processes and hammering (conversion of pigs to bars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pigs of iron are brought to forges composed of the finery and the chafery. In the finery pigs are softened and worked with long bars till they run together into a 'half-bloom', then beaten under a large water-powered hammer into rounds, reheated and worked until shaped into bars; final heatings and workings in the chafery produce bars of various shapes and sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow sequence of steps (softening, forming half-bloom, hammering, reheating, working in chafery). If any one process is omitted the iron will be deficient in toughness — toughness is considered the metal's perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting cast-iron for non-structural uses (and its brittleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sort of cast-iron is taken from receivers in great ladles and poured into moulds of fine sand for uses like backs of chimneys, hearths of ovens, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware this cast-iron is very brittle — if heated and struck with a hammer it breaks to pieces; restrict its use to purposes where brittleness is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cerusse (lead white) manufacture by fermentation in dung-heaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean soft lead is cast into thin plates, rolled so surfaces do not touch, put in pots suspended above vinegar, placed in beds of new horse-dung (400 pots per bed, 1600 per heap), covered and left about three weeks; plates unrolled and beaten to yield flakes which are then ground to fine powder and dried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key process points: surfaces must not touch (no cerusse grows where they do); vinegar corrodes the lead; dung quality and ordering critical — poor dung yields fuzzy, light, black or no flakes. After beating, grind with water between millstones to near impalpable fineness, then mould and sun-dry. There is variability: two identical pots may give very different yields; outsides near planks sometimes give larger flakes than insides near the rolls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health hazards and worker symptoms in cerusse manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Workmen suffer immediate stomach pain with contortions, costiveness resistant to cathartics, acute fevers, asthmas, dizziness, head pain, blindness, stupor, paralysis, loss of appetite, sickness, vomiting, and weakness — chiefly from mineral steams during casting and from dust during grinding and drying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize highest risk for those grinding and over the drying place; recommended treatments include lenitives, oil of olives, strong new wort, repeated clysters; be cautious of steams when taking up pots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saffron cultivation: soil, planting, spacing, and crop cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Best saffron heads planted in black rich sandy mould or mixed sandy land. Plough in early April and again at midsummer; spread 20 loads of rotten dung per acre and plough in; plant saffron-heads in rows 3 inches distant every way and 3 inches deep so heads lie 3 inches square; leave paths/trenches 2–3 yards apart for weeding/paring; dig up and replant midsummer following in new ground not used for saffron within seven years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain planting order over whole fields; hoe/pare and rake thin when heads spear (roughly a fortnight before Michaelmas); manage weeds to avoid choking flowers. Midsummer dig up and replant for crop rotation; practice repeats for second and third crops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saffron harvesting and kiln-drying (processing, kiln specification, and quality indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harvest flowers as soon as they appear, before fully blown (wet or dry). Pick sheaves clean of shells, sprinkle 2–3 fingers thick on double saffron-paper laid on hair-cloth in kiln, cover with saffron-papers, woollen cloth or baize, and a cushion; kiln heated with clean kindled charcoal/oven coals so hot fingers can hardly be kept between paper and hair-cloth; after an hour turn edges, loosen cake; if stuck wet paper with beer and dry; if still sticky dry with gentle heat and add 20–30 lb weight on kiln-board. Kiln frame: oaken, lathed, c.12 in square bottom, 2 ft high, 2 ft square top; inside lined with potter's clay and bottom clay hearth 4–5 in thick with hole for fire; outside plastered with lime and hair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality: best saffron has thick, short chives of high red shining colour inside and out. Beware burning or mixing with yellows inside shells; expected yield ~12 lbs per acre average (some years 20). 16 quarters of saffron-heads suffice to plant one acre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and classification of tin ores (pryan tin, mundic, white spar, 'Cornish diamonds')
rubrics_metrics.description: Tin stones sometimes found near surface or between rock walls in veins 4–18 inches broad; ores vary: rich/fat vs hungry/starved vs drossy substance. 'Pryan' tin (gravelly tin) is about half as rich as stone-derived tin. 'Mundic' ore (glittering deep brown) is thought to be a kind of sulphur that 'nourishes' tin but in excess indicates little tin and makes tin less ductile (brittle). White spar and other spars occur; 'Cornish diamonds' are a finer harder spar sometimes red and transparent like a deep ruby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize mundic by glittering brownness; presence affects ductility and processing; burning mundic gives a loathsome and dangerous stench and may produce arsenic-like smoke that yields vitriol when dissolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tin ore processing workflow (stamping, washing, grinding, drying, smelting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stones are broken and brought to a stamping-mill where they are arranged to be beaten small; washed into a latten-box with holes so ore falls near the mill while causalty (non-metalline parts) washed away. Remaining heavier material is re-washed, dried in furnace on iron plates, ground fine in crazing-mill, re-washed, slightly dried, then carried to blowing-house furnace to melt and cast. Dross floats on metal and is remelted with fresh ore; causalty heaps are left on banks and reworked after 6–7 years to extract further metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange progressive washing and re-washing to improve separation; dry and grind between processes; conserve dross for remelting; expect diminishing returns if causalty fetched over too soon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold refining with antimony: experimental procedure and expected outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Melt crown gold (examples: 178 grains of 22 carat) with large proportions of antimony (e.g., ~6 times by weight). Use borax in the pot to prevent sticking. Heat to clear light red, remove pot to cool and allow regulus to settle distinct from antimony. Break off regulus pieces for cupellation, remelt regulus with fresh antimony to increase separation. Recoveries noted (examples given: initial regulus weights and subsequent yields of fine gold after cupellation), with some measurable loss of gold overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect irregular gains/losses depending on whether regulus is remelted with same or fresh antimony; powdering, sparks during boiling, and effusion can cause loss. Save antimonial residues and process with tartar and nitre to recover remaining gold. Use borax to prevent sticking; cool in pots to aid separation rather than effusing into horns which may hinder separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold refining: cupellation, quartation, and alternatives (what they remove and limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cupellation with lead will free gold from baser metals but not from silver. For separation from silver, processes of quartation and parting by 'aquafortis' (nitric acid) are usual. Some refiners add antimony to colour fine gold for gilding, then remove antimony by strong heat and blast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose refining method based on impurity: use cupellation for base metals (copper, etc), use quartation/parting for silver. Be aware cupellation cannot remove silver; adding antimony for colour is practiced but requires subsequent rigorous refining.
